items.answer: (b) Violet and Red. When a narrow beam of white light passes through a prism, it splits up into a band of seven colours. Splitting of white light into its seven constituent (acronym VIBGYOR) colours on passing through a dispersive medium, i.e. the glass prism, is called dispersion of light. The order of deviation of colour from most to least is: Violet > Indigo > Blue > Green > Yellow > Orange > Red. Thus, here the colour P is Violet and colour Q is Red.

items.stem: What do you mean by dispersion of light? What is its cause?
items.answer: When white light is passed through a glass prism, it splits into its seven constituent colours (VIBGYOR). This phenomenon is called dispersion. Cause of dispersion: Light rays of different colours (or different wavelengths) travel at the same speed in vacuum or air. However, they travel with different speeds in a refractive medium like glass. The violet coloured ray travels with the least speed and the red ray with the maximum speed. Thus the refractive index of glass for violet colour is maximum and that for red is minimum. As a result, the different coloured rays bend differently on entering glass. The violet ray is deviated the most and the red the least, giving rise to the dispersion phenomenon.

items.stem: Draw a neat diagram to show the refraction of a light ray through a glass prism and label on it the angle of incidence and angle of deviation.

The ray bends towards the base of the prism on entering and again on leaving it, so the emergent ray FS is deviated from the direction of the incident ray PE by the angle of deviation ∠D.

items.stem: Describe the formation of rainbow in the sky with the help of a diagram.
items.answer: A rainbow is always formed in a direction opposite to that of the Sun. The water droplets act like small prisms. They refract and disperse the incident sunlight, then reflect it internally, and finally refract it again when it comes out of the droplet. Due to the dispersion of light and internal reflection, different colours reach the observer's eye.

items.stem: A star appears on the horizon. What is the true position of the star? Explain with the help of a diagram.
items.answer: The true position of the star is below the horizon. Incident rays from the star travel through the earth's atmosphere and reach the observer's eye. These incident rays travel from the rarer atmosphere to the denser atmosphere and bend towards the normal. Thus, they appear to come from a different position which is slightly upwards, so the star is seen above its true position.

items.stem: What is the scattering of light? Explain with the help of an example.
items.answer: The phenomenon of change in the direction of propagation of light caused by the large number of particles present in the atmosphere is called scattering of light. Example: The path of a beam of light becomes visible through a colloidal solution due to scattering of light.

items.stem: Why does the clear sky appear blue? OR Why does the colour of the sky appear blue? Explain in brief. OR Why does the sky look blue on a clear sunny day?
items.answer: The molecules of air and other fine particles in the atmosphere have a smaller size than the wavelength of visible light. These are more effective in scattering light of shorter wavelengths at the blue end than light of longer wavelength at the red end. Thus, the blue colour of the sky is due to the scattering of sunlight by fine particles in air.

items.stem: Give reason: (a) Danger signals are red. (b) We cannot see an object clearly if it is placed very close to the eyes.

items.stem: Name the part of the eye where the image is formed in a normal human eye. State how the image position changes in myopia and hypermetropia.
items.answer: Retina. In myopia the image of a distant object falls in front of the retina, and a concave lens brings the image back onto the retina; in hypermetropia the image of a nearby object falls behind the retina, and a convex lens brings the image onto the retina.

items.stem: Why is there no dispersion of light refracted through a rectangular glass slab?
items.answer: After refraction at the two parallel faces of a glass slab, a ray of light emerges in a direction parallel to the direction of incidence of the white light. As rays of all colours emerge in the same direction, i.e. the direction of incidence of the white light, there is no dispersion. However, there is lateral displacement.

items.stem: Why is it difficult to drive on a foggy day?
items.answer: On a foggy day, most of the light gets scattered by the particles in the fog and the visibility reduces, so it is difficult and dangerous to drive on a foggy day.

items.stem: Mention the factor on which scattering of light depends. Why does the sky appear dark in space?
items.answer: It depends on the presence of an atmosphere containing smoke particles, tiny water droplets, suspended particles of dust and molecules of air (and on the size of these particles relative to the wavelength of light). When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the beam becomes visible. The sky appears dark in space because there are no air molecules there to scatter light.

items.stem: A glass prism is able to produce a spectrum when white light passes through it but a glass slab does not produce any spectrum. Explain why it is so.
items.answer: When white light enters the glass slab, dispersion of light does take place: violet colour is refracted (bent) more than red colour on entering the glass slab. But all colours of light return to the original direction of propagation on refraction at the other, parallel face of the glass slab, and thus white light emerges out of the glass slab. Hence, a glass slab does not produce any spectrum, while a prism, whose faces are inclined, does.

items.stem: Why is Tyndall effect shown by colloidal particles? State four instances of observing the Tyndall effect.
items.answer:
Tyndall effect is shown by colloidal particles because they scatter light. Scattering of light is the change in the direction of light on striking an obstacle (atom, molecule, dust particle, smoke, water droplet, etc.). When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the light becomes visible. This phenomenon of scattering of light by colloidal particles is the Tyndall effect.
Four instances where the Tyndall effect can be observed:
1. When a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room, the smoke particles become visible due to scattering of light by these particles.
2. When sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest, the tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light.
3. Milk is a colloid that contains globules of fat and protein. When a beam of light is directed at a glass of milk the light is scattered — a good example of the Tyndall effect.
4. Blue colour of the clear sky: the scattering of the blue component of white light by the air molecules present in the atmosphere causes the blue colour of the sky.

items.stem: Explain, how the power of accommodation of human eye is achieved.
items.answer: The eye lens of the human eye is made up of a crystalline lens of variable focal length. The focal length of the human eye lens can be changed by the action of the ciliary muscles, so that images of objects placed at different positions are formed on the retina: the ciliary muscles relax for a distant object (the lens becomes thinner and its focal length increases) and contract for a nearby object (the lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases). This ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called the power of accommodation.

items.stem: With the help of ciliary muscles the human eye can change its curvature and thus alter the focal length of its lens. State the changes that occur in the curvature and focal length of the eye lens while viewing (i) a distant object, (ii) a nearby object. Explain, why a normal eye is not able to see distinctly the objects placed closer than 25 cm, without putting any strain on the eye.
items.answer:
(i) When we see distant objects, the ciliary muscles relax to decrease the curvature and thereby increase the focal length of the lens. Hence, the lens becomes thin. This enables us to see the distant object clearly. Thus, the focal length of the eye lens increases while seeing distant objects.
(ii) To see nearby objects clearly, the focal length of the lens should be shorter. For this, the ciliary muscles contract to increase the curvature and thereby decrease the focal length of the lens. Hence, the lens becomes thick. This enables us to see nearby objects clearly.
A normal eye is not able to see distinctly the objects placed closer than 25 cm without putting any strain on the eye. This is because the ciliary muscles of the eye are unable to contract beyond a certain limit; if the object is placed at a distance less than 25 cm from the eye, then the object appears blurred because the light rays coming from the object meet beyond the retina.

items.stem: The apparent altitude of stars appears to be generally more than their true altitudes. Explain, how.
items.answer: As we go up and up in the earth's atmosphere, it goes on becoming rarer and rarer. As a result, the atmospheric layer near the earth's surface has the maximum refractive index and the refractive index gradually decreases with increase in height. When a light ray from a star enters the earth's atmosphere, it travels from a rarer to a denser medium and hence continues to bend towards the normal. As a result, an observer on the earth considers the apparent position of the star to be at a higher altitude than its true position.

items.stem: State the cause of dispersion of white light by a glass prism. How did Newton, using two identical glass prisms, show that white light is made of seven colours? Draw a ray diagram to show the path of a narrow beam of white light through a combination of two identical prisms arranged together in inverted position with respect to each other when it is allowed to fall obliquely on one of the faces of the first prism of the combination.
items.answer:
Light is formed of different colours which travel at their own speed inside a prism. The colours therefore bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism — the red light bends the least while the violet bends the most — and this unequal bending causes dispersion.
Newton showed that the reverse of dispersion of light is also possible. He kept two prisms close to each other, one in the erect position and the other in an inverted position. The light gets dispersed when it passes through the first prism; the second prism receives all the seven coloured rays from the first prism and combines them into the original white light. This proves that white light is made of seven colours.

items.stem: What is dispersion of white light? State its cause. Draw a ray diagram to show the dispersion of white light by a glass prism.
items.answer:
Dispersion of white light: when a beam of white light is passed through a triangular glass prism, the white light splits up to form a band of seven colours on a white screen. This splitting of white light into seven colours on passing through a transparent medium like a glass prism is called dispersion of light.
Cause: the dispersion of white light occurs because the angle of refraction (or angle of deviation) of light of different colours is different when it passes through the glass prism. So when white light consisting of seven colours passes through a glass prism, each colour of it is refracted (or deviated) by a different angle, with the result that the seven colours are spread out to form a spectrum.

items.stem: Explain the common defects of eye, their causes and methods of correction.
items.answer:
The four most common types of defects of vision are :
(a) Myopia or near-sightedness. Causes of myopia : this defect arises due to either of the following two reasons — (i) the distance of the retina from the eye lens increases, (ii) the focal length of the eye lens becomes small. Correction of myopia : this defect can be corrected by using a concave lens of appropriate focal length.
(b) Hypermetropia or far-sightedness. Causes of hypermetropia : this defect arises due to either of the following two reasons — (i) the distance of the retina from the eye lens decreases, (ii) the focal length of the eye lens becomes large. Correction of hypermetropia : this defect can be corrected by a convex lens of appropriate power (or focal length).
(c) Presbyopia. Causes of presbyopia : this defect arises because the power of accommodation of the eye decreases due to the gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing of flexibility of the eye lens. Correction of presbyopia : this defect can be corrected by using bi-focal lenses. Its lower part consists of a convex lens which is used for reading purposes, whereas the upper part consists of a concave lens which is used for distant vision.
(d) Astigmatism. Causes of astigmatism : this defect is usually due to the cornea, which is not perfectly spherical and has different curvatures for horizontally and vertically lying objects. Correction of astigmatism : it can be corrected by using cylindrical lenses.

items.stem:
(a) What is myopia? State two causes of myopia. With the help of a labelled ray diagram show the correction of myopia using appropriate lens.
(b) The near point of a myopic eye is 1 m. Find the power of the lens required to correct this defect. Assume that near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
items.answer:
(a) Myopia is a defect of vision in which the eye can see only nearby objects clearly; the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina, so distant objects appear blurred.
Causes of myopia: (i) elongation of the eye ball; (ii) the focal length of the eye lens becomes too short.
Correction: a concave lens of suitable power diverges the rays coming from a distant object before they reach the eye lens, so that the eye lens forms the image on the retina.
(b) v = −1 m = −100 cm (the defective near point), u = −25 cm (near point of the normal eye)
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
(−1/100) − (−1/25) = 1/f
1/f = 3/100
f = 100/3 = 33.3 cm
P = 1/f = +3 D, i.e. a convex lens of power +3 D.

items.stem:
(a) A student suffering from myopia is not able to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m. List two possible reasons due to which this defect of vision have arisen. With the help of ray diagrams, explain (i) why the student is unable to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m from his eyes, (ii) the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision and how this defect is corrected by the use of this lens.
(b) If in this case, the numerical value of the focal length of the corrective lens is 5 m, find the power of the lens as per the new cartesian sign convention.
items.answer:
(a) Two possible reasons for this defect: elongation of the eye ball (the retina moves away from the eye lens), and excessive curvature of the eye lens so that its focal length becomes too short.
(i) The student is unable to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m from his eyes because he is suffering from myopia, wherein a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly — rays from a distant object are brought to a focus in front of the retina.
(ii) A concave lens can be used as the corrective lens to restore proper vision. A concave lens of suitable power will diverge the incoming rays and thus bring the image back on to the retina, and the defect is corrected.
(b) For a myopic eye the corrective lens is concave, so by the new cartesian sign convention f = −5 m.
P = 1/f = 1/(−5) = −0.2 D

items.stem: What is atmospheric refraction ? Use this phenomenon to explain the following natural events : (a) Twinkling of stars, (b) Advanced sun-rise and delayed sun-set. Draw diagrams to illustrate your answers.
items.answer:
Atmospheric refraction : the refraction of light caused by the earth's atmosphere (having air layers of varying optical densities) is called atmospheric refraction.
(a) Twinkling of stars : atmospheric pressure (and hence density) keeps on decreasing considerably with altitude, so the upper layers of the atmosphere are optically rarer than the lower layers. The rays of light suffer refraction at each layer of the atmosphere and bend slightly. Thus, each ray of light from the star follows a curved path to reach the observer; a ray from a star at X appears to come from a star at X′, i.e. the star appears to be higher in the sky. Due to wind and convection currents, the density of the atmospheric layers keeps on changing, so the apparent position of the star keeps fluctuating about its mean position. This fluctuating image of the star makes it appear to twinkle to the observer.
(b) Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset : the sun is visible before the actual sunrise and after the actual sunset. Air near the earth is optically denser than that at higher altitudes. The sun's rays, while travelling to reach the surface of the earth, suffer refraction at each layer as they travel from a rarer to a denser medium. Due to these bent rays, the sun appears higher above the horizon than it actually is. Therefore the sun becomes visible about 2 minutes before its actual sunrise and remains visible for about 2 minutes after its actual sunset.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by dispersion of white light ? Describe the formation of rainbow in the sky with the help of a diagram. (b) What is hypermetropia ? Draw ray diagrams to show the image formation of an object by (i) Hypermetropic eye. (ii) Correction made with a suitable lens for hypermetropic eye.
items.answer:
(a) Dispersion : the process of splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours is called dispersion. The band of seven colours formed on a screen due to the dispersion of white light is called the spectrum of visible light (spectrum of white light).
Rainbow : the rainbow is the spectrum of sunlight in nature. When the atmosphere is heavily moisture laden (at the time of rain), spherical water droplets act as prisms and refract the sunlight to lead to the formation of a rainbow. Parallel beams of light coming from the sun get dispersed at the first surface of a water droplet, suffer total internal reflection at the second surface and are refracted again on emerging, producing a cone of rays at the observer's eye. The rainbow therefore appears as an arc of a circle for an observer on the earth.
(b) Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is the defect of the human eye in which a person can see clearly objects at large distances, but cannot see nearby objects clearly. In such an eye the image of a nearby object is formed behind the retina. Correction : it is corrected by using spectacles having a convex lens, which converges the rays and shifts the image from beyond the retina on to the retina. A person suffering from both myopia and hypermetropia has to wear spectacles having bifocal lenses — the upper half is a concave lens for distant vision and the lower half is a convex lens for reading.

items.stem: (i) Draw a ray diagram to explain the term angle of deviation. (ii) Why do the component colours of incident white light split into a spectrum while passing through a glass prism, explain. (iii) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the formation of a rainbow.
items.answer:
(i) When a ray of light passes through a glass prism, the emergent ray bends at an angle to the direction of the incident ray, and the angle between the direction of the incident ray and that of the emergent ray is known as the angle of deviation.
(ii) The splitting of the light ray occurs because of the different angles of bending of each colour: each colour passing through the prism bends through a different angle with respect to the incident beam (red bends the least, violet the most). This gives rise to the formation of the colour spectrum.
(iii) Rainbow formation : sunlight entering a spherical raindrop is refracted and dispersed at the first surface, totally internally reflected at the inner back surface, and refracted again as it leaves the drop, so the dispersed colours reach the observer's eye as an arc — red on the outside and violet on the inside of the bow. (Labelled ray diagram as shown.)

items.stem: A student finds the writing on the black board as blurred and unclear when sitting on the last desk in a classroom. He however, sees it clearly when sitting on the front desk at an approximate distance of 2 m from the black board. (a) Draw ray diagram to illustrate the formation of image of the black board writing by his eye-lens when he is seated at the (i) last desk, (ii) front desk. (b) Name the kind of lens that would help him to see clearly even when he is seated at the last desk. Draw a ray diagram to illustrate how this lens helps him to see clearly.
items.answer:
(a) (i) For the student sitting at the last desk the eye lens forms the image of the blackboard writing in front of the retina, so the writing appears blurred (figure). (ii) For the student sitting at the front desk, about 2 m from the board, the image is formed on the retina itself and the writing is seen clearly (figure).
(b) The student is suffering from myopia, so his eye defect can be corrected by using a concave lens of suitable focal length. The concave lens first diverges the rays coming from the distant blackboard, so that they appear to come from a nearer position (where the blackboard appears to be); the eye lens then forms the image on the retina and he sees the writing clearly even from the last desk.

... known as dispersion. He concluded that white light is a mixture of light of various colours and identified red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
All colours of light travel at the same speed in a vacuum. When they enter a transparent substance like glass, they all slow down but by different amounts. Because they slow down, they are refracted but because they slow down by different amounts, different colours are refracted through different angles.
(i) Where in nature can you find evidence that white sunlight may be made of different colours?
(ii) When a monochromatic light passes through a prism, will it show dispersion?
items.answer:
(i) The formation of a rainbow in the sky is the natural evidence that white sunlight is made of different colours.
(ii) No, a monochromatic light will not show any dispersion; it will only show deviation.

items.stem:
The ciliary muscles of eye control the curvature of the lens in the eye and hence can alter the effective focal length of the system. When the muscles are fully relaxed, the focal length is maximum. When the muscles are strained the curvature of lens increases (that means radius of curvature decreases) and focal length decreases. For a clear vision the image must be on retina. The image distance is therefore fixed for clear vision and it equals the distance of retina from eye-lens. It is about 2.5 cm for a grown-up person. A person can theoretically have clear vision of objects situated at any large distance from the eye. The smallest distance at which a person can clearly see is related to minimum possible focal length. The ciliary muscles are most strained in this position. For an average grown-up person minimum distance of object should be around 25 cm.
A person suffering from eye defects uses spectacles (eye glass). The function of lens of spectacles is to form the image of the objects within the range in which person can see clearly. The image of the spectacle-lens becomes object for eye-lens and whose image is formed on retina. The number of spectacle-lens used for the remedy of eye defect is decided by the power of the lens required, and the number of spectacle-lens is equal to the numerical value of the power of lens with sign. For example, if power of lens required is +3 D (converging lens of focal length 100/3 cm) then number of lens will be +3.
For all the calculations required you can use the lens formula and lens maker's formula. Assume that the eye lens is equiconvex lens. Neglect the distance between eye lens and the spectacle lens.
(i) What do you mean by the ciliary muscles?
(ii) What is the minimum focal length of eye lens of a normal person?
(iii) What is the maximum focal length of eye lens of normal person?
(iv) A near-sighted man can clearly see object only up-to a distance of 100 cm and not beyond this. What is the number of the spectacles lens necessary for the remedy of this defect?
items.answer:
(i) The muscles which are used to change the focal length of the eye lens by changing the radii of curvature of the lens are known as the ciliary muscles.
(ii) 25/11 cm (about 2.27 cm). Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with v = +2.5 cm (the retina, a fixed image distance) and the nearest object at u = -x: 1/f = 1/2.5 + 1/x. f is minimum when x is minimum, i.e. x = 25 cm, so 1/f(min) = 1/2.5 + 1/25.
(iii) 2.5 cm. f is maximum when x is maximum, i.e. u = -infinity, so 1/f(max) = 1/2.5 + 1/(infinity) = 1/2.5.
(iv) For the near-sighted man the spectacle lens must form the image of a distant object within his 100 cm range. For the lens, u = -infinity and v = -100 cm, so 1/f = 1/(-100) - 1/(-infinity), giving f = -100 cm = -1 m and P = 1/f(m) = -1 D. Hence the number of the spectacle lens needed is -1 (a diverging lens).
